lesson.title: Zijn & Hebben
lesson.subtitle: to be, to have, and the Dutch way to say your age

hook.title: The Two Verbs Every Sentence Leans On
hook.content: Zijn (to be) and hebben (to have) carry most of the weight. Ik ben, jij bent, hij is; ik heb, jij hebt, hij heeft. With these two verbs, the early vocabulary turns into real sentences.

pattern.title: Age is something you are
pattern.content: Dutch says ik ben twintig for 'I am twenty'. Age belongs to zijn, not hebben. Possession belongs to hebben: ik heb een boek. Keep the two frames apart and the rest of the tense system will stand on them.
pattern.linguist_note: Zijn and hebben are the Dutch reflexes of the same West Germanic being and having verbs that gave English is and have.
pattern.trap_note: Never say ik heb twintig jaar for your age. Dutch uses zijn for age, even though English sometimes says 'I have twenty years' in other languages.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Zijn & Hebben):
exercises.target_answer: zijn, hebben, ik, jij, hij, twintig
exercises.meaning: to be, to have, I, you (informal singular), he, twenty
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Zijn & Hebben": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik ben twintig.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Zijn & Hebben”.

cues: The pattern: Age is something you are
It means: You have a book.
exercises.explanation: “Jij hebt een boek.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Age is something you are.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Never say ik heb twintig jaar for your age. Dutch uses zijn for age, even though English sometimes says 'I have twenty years' in other languages.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Hij is hier.” is word-for-word “He is here.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Age is something you are.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Wij hebben water.” reuses only material taught in “Zijn & Hebben” — Age is something you are.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Wij hebben water.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Age is something you are.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I am hungry.”
twist.explanation: Dutch says 'I have hunger' for being hungry; honger is the noun inside the hebben frame.

foreshadow.line: Both verbs will need an article system to stand on. De and het are next.

summary.outcome: Use zijn and hebben in the singular and plural and say your age with zijn.
summary.takeaway: Two verbs, two frames: being takes zijn, possession takes hebben, and age belongs to being.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Zijn & Have Gym.

zijn.etymology_derivation: The being verb is irregular in every Germanic language; English is and Dutch is are the same old root.

hebben.etymology_derivation: English have and Dutch hebben descend from the same verb; the b is preserved.

ik.etymology_derivation: The same pronoun as English I, worn differently; German has its own form.

jij.etymology_derivation: Dutch keeps the old singular thou as jij; English lost it outside dialect and poetry.

hij.etymology_derivation: The same pronoun family as English he; the final sound has softened.

twintig.etymology_derivation: English twenty and Dutch twintig are the same word; age uses zijn.
